title: Embodied Books
abstract: «We often speak of the body of text, and Darian Goldin Stahl’s excellent and timely book deals with sister-inspired texts of the body. Stahl makes the case, beautifully and powerfully, for the value of artists’ books to open us up (like a laparotomy) to illness experience.» (Paul Crawford, Professor of Health Humanities, University of Nottingham, UK) This book investigates how handmade artists’ books excite the senses to communicate lived experiences of illness and disability. The combination of text, image, materials, and form, along with the gesture of turning pages, make artists’ books a powerful source of expressive potential. These works of art not only enable patients to create meaning from their medical experiences, but also invite healthcare learners to an uncensored read of critiques on Western medicine. Artists’ books are increasingly popular among medical institutions in an age of digital screens because of their intimate handheld, multi-sensory expressions of bodily phenomena that may be difficult or impossible to communicate through words alone. By applying a phenomenological practice of sensing and meaning-making, the author provides step-by-step instructions for creating new artists’ books as part of health humanities pedagogies. In this way, Embodied Books serves as a philosophical and pragmatic example of why and how experiencing artists’ books in healthcare contexts is so important.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Embodied Books (2024) is a recent scholarly monograph examining how handmade artists' books engage the senses to communicate lived experiences of illness and disability. Published in the Medical Humanities series at Peter Lang Verlag, the work has begun to circulate in educational contexts, with documented teaching use and library holdings. Citation accumulation is still in its earliest stages, reflecting the book's recent publication date rather than lack of scholarly merit.

Full narrative

Darian Goldin Stahl's Embodied Books investigates the intersection of material book arts, embodied cognition, and health humanities—a timely contribution to scholarship that bridges artistic practice and lived experience of disability and illness. The work draws on the theoretical foundation that handmade artists' books, through their tactile and sensory properties, can open readers to dimensions of illness experience that conventional texts cannot access. This argument is framed around the concept of embodied knowledge, positioning the physical artifact of the book itself as a medium of communication rather than mere container.

The book appears early in its scholarly lifecycle, with no citations yet recorded in OpenAlex. However, the absence of citations at this stage reflects the work's 2024 publication date rather than lack of scholarly or professional recognition. More informative are the emerging signals of pedagogical adoption and professional engagement. The work has been presented by the author in a recorded lecture through the University of Toronto's Continuing Professional Development program in the Faculty of Medicine, and holds two library locations in Open Library, indicating acquisition by academic institutions. These signals suggest the work is beginning to reach educators and students in health humanities and medical humanities curricula.

Embodied Books sits within the "Medical Humanities: Criticism and Creativity" series (ISSN 2504-5229), positioning it alongside peer volumes such as Breast Cancer Inside Out (2021) and Moving along (2023). This series placement situates the work within an established conversation about artistic and creative approaches to health and medicine—a field where accessibility to lived experience and alternative modes of representation are increasingly recognized as scholarly contributions.

The work demonstrates alignment with Quality Education (SDG 4) in its framing, suggesting relevance to educational accessibility and inclusive pedagogies. Though formal citation metrics remain at zero, the early teaching adoption and professional library acquisition indicate the work is functioning as a pedagogical anchor in medical humanities and health studies contexts. As the work matures in the scholarly record, its influence on research, teaching, and creative practice in health humanities will become more fully traceable.
